studyMetadata.title: The Story of the Bible: New Testament
studyMetadata.subtitle: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule
studyMetadata.description: The second half of the Bible’s story, traced through eight key passages: the arrival of the King, the cross and resurrection, the Spirit and the new people of God, and the hope of a new creation. Part 2 of 2: it picks up where the Old Testament study ends, and works for readers new to the Bible’s big picture and for those who already know the stories.
studyMetadata.author: Rick Creighton

elements.text:
Welcome to the second half of the Bible’s story. This study traces the New Testament in eight key passages, and it picks up where the Old Testament study ends. If you have not done that study, the next few paragraphs will bring you up to date.

Work through the questions alone or with your group. Tap the verse reference above a question to read the passage. When you have written an answer, tap Check [[icon:localValidate]] to see how it compares with what the passage says. At the end of each session, tap Read more to go deeper.

elements.question: If a great king were born today, how would you expect the news to be announced, and who would be told first?

elements.text:
The story so far: The Bible is one story about a King and his kingdom: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule. In Eden that kingdom was perfect. It was lost when humans rebelled, but God promised to restore it. He promised Abraham a people, a land and blessing for the nations. He rescued Israel from Egypt, gave them his law, and promised David a king whose rule would last for ever. Yet Israel fell into exile, and the prophets looked ahead to a new covenant, a suffering servant, a Son of Man given an everlasting kingdom, and a new creation.

Then the Old Testament falls silent. For about four hundred years the promises wait. The New Testament begins in a small corner of the Roman empire with the announcement that the wait is over.

elements.question: Tap to see what these three titles mean.
elements.answer: Three titles for Jesus come up in this session. Saviour means one who rescues. Christ is the Greek form of ‘Messiah’, the anointed king God promised. Lord means master and ruler, and in the Greek Old Testament it is also the word used for God’s own name. Together they say who Jesus is and what he has come to do.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Luke 1:1–25 to see how Luke begins his Gospel and how the birth of John the Baptist is announced. Then read Matthew 1:1–17, which traces Jesus’ family line back through David to Abraham.

Luke 1:1–25 (NET)

1Now many have undertaken to compile an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, 2like the accounts passed on to us by those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word from the beginning. 3So it seemed good to me as well, because I have followed all things carefully from the beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, 4so that you may know for certain the things you were taught.

5During the reign of Herod king of Judea, there lived a priest named Zechariah who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, and he had a wife named Elizabeth, who was a descendant of Aaron. 6They were both righteous in the sight of God, following all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly. 7But they did not have a child, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both very old.

8Now while Zechariah was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, 9he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the Holy Place of the Lord and burn incense. 10Now the whole crowd of people were praying outside at the hour of the incense offering. 11An angel of the Lord, standing on the right side of the altar of incense, appeared to him. 12And Zechariah, visibly shaken when he saw the angel, was seized with fear. 13But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son; you will name him John. 14Joy and gladness will come to you, and many will rejoice at his birth, 15for he will be great in the sight of the Lord. He must never drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth.

16He will turn many of the people of Israel to the Lord their God. 17And he will go as forerunner before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers back to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared for him.”

18Zechariah said to the angel, “How can I be sure of this? For I am an old man, and my wife is old as well.” 19The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. 20And now, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time, you will be silent, unable to speak, until the day these things take place.”

21Now the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they began to wonder why he was delayed in the Holy Place. 22When he came out, he was not able to speak to them. They realized that he had seen a vision in the Holy Place, because he was making signs to them and remained unable to speak. 23When his time of service was over, he went to his home.

24After some time his wife Elizabeth became pregnant, and for five months she kept herself in seclusion. She said, 25“This is what the Lord has done for me at the time when he has been gracious to me, to take away my disgrace among people.”

Matthew 1:1–17 (NET)

1This is the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.

2Abraham was the father of Isaac, Isaac the father of Jacob, Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, 3Judah the father of Perez and Zerah (by Tamar), Perez the father of Hezron, Hezron the father of Ram, 4Ram the father of Amminadab, Amminadab the father of Nahshon, Nahshon the father of Salmon, 5Salmon the father of Boaz (by Rahab), Boaz the father of Obed (by Ruth), Obed the father of Jesse, 6and Jesse the father of David the king. David was the father of Solomon (by the wife of Uriah),

7Solomon the father of Rehoboam, Rehoboam the father of Abijah, Abijah the father of Asa, 8Asa the father of Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, Joram the father of Uzziah, 9Uzziah the father of Jotham, Jotham the father of Ahaz, Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, 10Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, Manasseh the father of Amon, Amon the father of Josiah, 11and Josiah the father of Jeconiah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon.

12After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah became the father of Shealtiel, Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, 13Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, Abiud the father of Eliakim, Eliakim the father of Azor, 14Azor the father of Zadok, Zadok the father of Achim, Achim the father of Eliud, 15Eliud the father of Eleazar, Eleazar the father of Matthan, Matthan the father of Jacob, 16and Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, by whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.

17So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations.

elements.passageText:
26In the sixth month of Elizabeth’s pregnancy, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a town of Galilee called Nazareth, 27to a virgin engaged to a man whose name was Joseph, a descendant of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. 28The angel came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one, the Lord is with you!” 29But she was greatly troubled by his words and began to wonder about the meaning of this greeting. 30So the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God! 31Listen: You will become pregnant and give birth to a son, and you will name him Jesus. 32He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David. 33He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will never end.”

34Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I have not been intimate with a man?” 35The angel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called the Son of God. 36“And look, your relative Elizabeth has also become pregnant with a son in her old age—although she was called barren, she is now in her sixth month! 37For nothing will be impossible with God.” 38So Mary said, “Yes, I am a servant of the Lord; let this happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.

elements.question: What does the angel say about who this child will be and what he will do (verses 31–33)?
elements.questionHint: Notice the words ‘throne’, ‘David’ and ‘for ever’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The boy is to be named Jesus and is described as great and as the Son of God. Gabriel says God will make him the king that David’s throne has been waiting for, ruling Jacob’s people without any limit of time. His kingdom will have no end. So he is the royal descendant of David that God had promised.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **the promised king of David’s line**, the Son of God, whose kingdom will never end.
keyTerms: great|son of the most high|son of god

elements.question: How does Mary respond, and what does the angel say will bring about the birth (verses 34–38)?
elements.questionHint: Look at Mary’s question in verse 34 and at the angel’s answer.
elements.sampleAnswer: Mary is baffled, because as a virgin she cannot see how she could become a mother. Gabriel replies that the Holy Spirit will work in her, making the baby holy, God’s own Son. She does not resist. She calls herself the Lord’s servant and accepts the message.
elements.mainPoint: The child comes **by God’s power**, and Mary responds with trusting obedience.
keyTerms: virgin|how can this be|how will this be
holy spirit|power of the most high|overshadow

elements.passageText:
8Now there were shepherds nearby living out in the field, keeping guard over their flock at night. 9An angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were absolutely terrified. 10But the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid! Listen carefully, for I proclaim to you good news that brings great joy to all the people: 11Today your Savior is born in the city of David. He is Christ the Lord. 12This will be a sign for you: You will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth and lying in a manger.”

13Suddenly a vast, heavenly army appeared with the angel, praising God and saying, 14“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people with whom he is pleased!”

elements.question: Who receives the first announcement of the birth, and how do they react?
elements.questionHint: Look at who they are, where they are, and what the angel says in verse 10.
elements.sampleAnswer: Shepherds watching their flocks at night are the first to be told. An angel appears and the glory of the Lord shines around them, which makes them terrified. The angel calms them: he has good news that will bring great joy to the entire population.
elements.mainPoint: The good news comes first to **ordinary shepherds**, and it is for all the people.

elements.question: What three titles does the angel give the baby in verse 11, and how is he to be recognised in verse 12?
elements.questionHint: The three titles come together at the end of verse 11.
elements.sampleAnswer: Three titles are given to the baby: Saviour, Christ and Lord, and he is said to be born in David’s town. They mark him out as rescuer, promised king and ruler. The identifying sign is humble: a newborn wrapped in cloths and laid in a feeding trough.
elements.mainPoint: The baby is **Saviour, Christ and Lord**, yet he is found in a manger.

elements.question: What do the angels say in verses 13–14 about God and about people on earth?
elements.questionHint: Notice the two directions of the song: heaven and earth.
elements.sampleAnswer: A huge crowd of angels praise God, wishing him glory in the heights of heaven. They also announce peace on earth for people who have God’s favour. So the birth honours God and benefits people, which is what the kingdom is for.
elements.mainPoint: The birth brings **glory to God and peace to people**.

elements.question: What contrast do you see between what is said about this child and the way he arrives?
elements.questionHint: Compare ‘throne’ and ‘Lord’ with the place and the people mentioned.
elements.sampleAnswer: The child is called Son of the Most High, Lord and Christ, with an everlasting throne. Yet his mother is a young woman from a small town, his bed is a manger, and the first people to hear are shepherds. The King comes quietly and in humility, not with outward splendour. The kingdom has begun, but not in the way anyone would have predicted.
elements.mainPoint: **The King arrives in humility**: great titles, yet a manger and shepherds.

elements.question: Mary’s answer in verse 38 is a simple yes to God. Where might God be asking you to trust his word and say yes?
The first news went to shepherds, people with little status. What does that tell you about who the good news is for? Who might your church be overlooking?

elements.text:
The King has come. The promises to David, to Abraham and to the whole world are beginning to be kept, and the first sign is a baby in a manger. Next session we see this King begin his public work.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: The King has been born. Now, about thirty years later, he begins his public work. Mark’s Gospel gets to the point very quickly.

elements.question: What is the best news you have ever received? How did you respond when you heard it?

elements.text:
Since last time: Very little is recorded of Jesus’ first thirty years. The Gospels tell of visitors from the east who came to worship the infant King, and of the family’s flight to Egypt to escape a jealous Herod. Luke tells of Jesus at the age of twelve in the temple, talking about his ‘Father’s house’. After that, he grows up in Nazareth as a carpenter’s son.

Mark skips all of this. His Gospel starts with a prophet in the wilderness, and moves at once to Jesus himself.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Matthew 2 (the visitors from the east, and the escape to Egypt) and Luke 2:41–52 (Jesus at twelve in the temple).

Matthew 2 (NET)

1After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, in the time of King Herod, wise men from the East came to Jerusalem 2saying, “Where is the one who is born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” 3When King Herod heard this he was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him. 4After assembling all the chief priests and experts in the law, he asked them where the Christ was to be born. 5“In Bethlehem of Judea,” they said, “for it is written this way by the prophet: 6‘And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are in no way least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’”

7Then Herod privately summoned the wise men and determined from them when the star had appeared. 8He sent them to Bethlehem and said, “Go and look carefully for the child. When you find him, inform me so that I can go and worship him as well.” 9After listening to the king they left, and once again the star they saw when it rose led them until it stopped above the place where the child was. 10When they saw the star they shouted joyfully. 11As they came into the house and saw the child with Mary his mother, they bowed down and worshiped him. They opened their treasure boxes and gave him gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh. 12After being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back by another route to their own country.

13After they had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Get up, take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod is going to look for the child to kill him.” 14Then he got up, took the child and his mother during the night, and went to Egypt. 15He stayed there until Herod died. In this way what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet was fulfilled: “I called my Son out of Egypt.”

16When Herod saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, he became enraged. He sent men to kill all the children in Bethlehem and throughout the surrounding region from the age of two and under, according to the time he had learned from the wise men. 17Then what was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: 18“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud wailing, Rachel weeping for her children, and she did not want to be comforted, because they were gone.”

19After Herod had died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt 20saying, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life are dead.” 21So he got up and took the child and his mother and returned to the land of Israel. 22But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. After being warned in a dream, he went to the regions of Galilee. 23He came to a town called Nazareth and lived there. Then what had been spoken by the prophets was fulfilled, that Jesus would be called a Nazarene.

Luke 2:41–52 (NET)

41Now Jesus’ parents went to Jerusalem every year for the Feast of the Passover. 42When he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom. 43But when the feast was over, as they were returning home, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, 44but (because they assumed that he was in their group of travelers) they went a day’s journey. Then they began to look for him among their relatives and acquaintances. 45When they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem to look for him. 46After three days they found him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. 47And all who heard Jesus were astonished at his understanding and his answers. 48When his parents saw him, they were overwhelmed. His mother said to him, “Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been looking for you anxiously.”

49But he replied, “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” 50Yet his parents did not understand the remark he made to them. 51Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. But his mother kept all these things in her heart.

52And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and with people.

elements.question: Tap to see what ‘gospel’ means.
elements.answer: ‘Gospel’ means ‘good news’. In the ancient world the word was used for a royal announcement, such as the news of a king’s victory or accession. Mark’s book begins with the words ‘the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ’: the good news is that the King has come. The four books about Jesus’ life in the New Testament are called Gospels because they tell this news.

elements.passageText:
1The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. 2As it is written in the prophet Isaiah, “Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way, 3the voice of one shouting in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make his paths straight.’” 4In the wilderness John the baptizer began preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. 5People from the whole Judean countryside and all of Jerusalem were going out to him, and he was baptizing them in the Jordan River as they confessed their sins. 6John wore a garment made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. 7He proclaimed, “One more powerful than I am is coming after me; I am not worthy to bend down and untie the strap of his sandals. 8I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

9Now in those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan River. 10And just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens splitting apart and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. 11And a voice came from heaven: “You are my one dear Son; in you I take great delight.”

12The Spirit immediately drove him into the wilderness. 13He was in the wilderness forty days, enduring temptations from Satan. He was with wild animals, and angels were ministering to his needs.

14Now after John was imprisoned, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God. 15He said, “The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe the gospel!”

elements.question: How does Mark introduce the story, and what is John the Baptist’s role (verses 1–8)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the first verse and at the words quoted from the prophets.
elements.sampleAnswer: Mark opens by announcing the good news about Jesus Christ, the Son of God, which the prophets had pointed to. John is the messenger who gets people ready: he calls them to repent, to be baptised and to admit their sins, from all over the region. He tells the crowds that a more powerful person is following him, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit.
elements.mainPoint: The gospel is **about Jesus Christ, the Son of God**, announced by the prophets and prepared by John.

elements.question: What happens at Jesus’ baptism, and what does the voice from heaven say (verses 9–11)?
elements.questionHint: Notice the heavens, the Spirit and the voice.
elements.sampleAnswer: John baptises Jesus in the Jordan. As Jesus rises from the water, the heavens split open and the Spirit settles on him like a dove. God speaks: Jesus is his one dear Son, and God is delighted with him. In one moment the Father names his Son and equips him with the Spirit.
elements.mainPoint: God publicly names Jesus **his dear Son** and gives him the Spirit.

elements.question: What happens straight after the baptism (verses 12–13)?
elements.questionHint: Notice who sends Jesus into the wilderness and who is waiting for him there.
elements.sampleAnswer: At once the Spirit drives Jesus out into the desert, where he spends forty days being tempted by Satan. He lives among wild animals, and angels look after him. The Son who has just been named by God immediately faces the enemy.
elements.mainPoint: The Son **faces the enemy** straight away, and he does not face him alone.

elements.question: What does Jesus announce in verses 14–15, and how does he say people should respond?
elements.questionHint: Look for the four short statements in verse 15.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus comes to Galilee proclaiming the good news of God. He says the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near. The right response is to repent and to believe the good news. The long wait is over, and a new stage of the story has begun.
elements.mainPoint: The time is fulfilled: **God’s kingdom is near**, and people are to repent and believe.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Jesus says ‘the time is fulfilled’. Which promises from the Old Testament study do you think he has in mind?

elements.question: Mark begins with ‘the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God’. List what this passage shows about who Jesus is.
elements.questionHint: Look at the title in verse 1, what John says, the voice from heaven and what Jesus says.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, announced in advance by the prophets. He is more powerful than John, and will baptise with the Holy Spirit. God declares him his one dear Son and fills him with the Spirit. He faces Satan in the wilderness, and he comes announcing that the kingdom of God is near.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **the Christ, the Son of God**, who brings the kingdom.

elements.question: Jesus calls people to repent and believe. What does repentance look like in your own life at the moment?
God says ‘You are my one dear Son’ before Jesus has done any miracles or teaching. What does that say about how God sees his people? How do you tend to see your own worth?

elements.text:
The King has arrived and announced his kingdom. But a King must win his kingdom, and the Old Testament has told us how: through a servant who suffers. In the next session we meet the risen Jesus, and learn how all the Scriptures point to him.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: Jesus has been crucified, and on the third day he rises. This session we join two of his disciples on the road home, as he shows them what the whole Bible is about.

elements.question: Has a disappointment ever turned out to be part of a bigger plan? What did it look like at the time, and what did you see later?

elements.text:
Since last time: Jesus spent about three years teaching, healing and calling people to follow him. He chose twelve disciples, taught about the kingdom in parables, and showed God’s power over disease, evil spirits and even death. Many were amazed, but the religious leaders opposed him. At Passover in Jerusalem he was arrested, tried and crucified, and buried in a tomb. This was the suffering Isaiah had spoken of, though few of his followers saw it at the time.

Early on the third day, women found the tomb empty. Our passage begins on that same day.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Luke 23:26–24:12 (the crucifixion, burial and the empty tomb). For the wider ministry, read Mark 8:27–9:1, where Peter calls Jesus the Christ and Jesus speaks of his coming suffering.

Luke 23:26–24:12 (NET)

26As they led him away, they seized Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country. They placed the cross on his back and made him carry it behind Jesus. 27A great number of the people followed him, among them women who were mourning and wailing for him. 28But Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. 29For this is certain: The days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore children, and the breasts that never nursed!’ 30Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us!’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us!’ 31For if such things are done when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

32Two other criminals were also led away to be executed with him. 33So when they came to the place that is called “The Skull,” they crucified him there, along with the criminals, one on his right and one on his left. 34[But Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.”] Then they threw dice to divide his clothes. 35The people also stood there watching, but the leaders ridiculed him, saying, “He saved others. Let him save himself if he is the Christ of God, his chosen one!” 36The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine, 37and saying, “If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!” 38There was also an inscription over him, “This is the king of the Jews.”

39One of the criminals who was hanging there railed at him, saying, “Aren’t you the Christ? Save yourself and us!” 40But the other rebuked him, saying, “Don’t you fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? 41And we rightly so, for we are getting what we deserve for what we did, but this man has done nothing wrong.” 42Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingdom.” 43And Jesus said to him, “I tell you the truth, today you will be with me in paradise.”

44It was now about noon, and darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon, 45because the sun’s light failed. The temple curtain was torn in two. 46Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” And after he said this he breathed his last.

47Now when the centurion saw what had happened, he praised God and said, “Certainly this man was innocent!” 48And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts. 49And all those who knew Jesus stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee saw these things.

50Now there was a man named Joseph who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man. 51(He had not consented to their plan and action.) He was from the Judean town of Arimathea, and was looking forward to the kingdom of God. 52He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. 53Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and placed it in a tomb cut out of the rock, where no one had yet been buried. 54It was the day of preparation and the Sabbath was beginning. 55The women who had accompanied Jesus from Galilee followed, and they saw the tomb and how his body was laid in it. 56Then they returned and prepared aromatic spices and perfumes. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

24:1Now on the first day of the week, at early dawn, the women went to the tomb, taking the aromatic spices they had prepared. 2They found that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, 3but when they went in, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. 4While they were perplexed about this, suddenly two men stood beside them in dazzling attire. 5The women were terribly frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, but the men said to them, “Why do you look for the living among the dead? 6He is not here, but has been raised! Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, 7that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.” 8Then the women remembered his words,

9and when they returned from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. 10Now it was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles. 11But these words seemed like pure nonsense to them, and they did not believe them. 12But Peter got up and ran to the tomb. He bent down and saw only the strips of linen cloth; then he went home, wondering what had happened.

Mark 8:27–9:1 (NET)

27Then Jesus and his disciples went to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” 28They said, “John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and still others, one of the prophets.” 29He asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” 30Then he warned them not to tell anyone about him.

31Then Jesus began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and experts in the law, and be killed, and after three days rise again. 32He spoke openly about this. So Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. 33But after turning and looking at his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan. You are not setting your mind on God’s interests, but on man’s.”

34Then Jesus called the crowd, along with his disciples, and said to them, “If anyone wants to become my follower, he must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. 35For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life because of me and because of the gospel will save it. 36For what benefit is it for a person to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his life? 37What can a person give in exchange for his life? 38For if anyone is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.” 9:1And he said to them, “I tell you the truth, there are some standing here who will not experience death before they see the kingdom of God come with power.”

elements.term: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms
elements.question: Tap to see what Jesus means.
elements.answer: This was a way of naming the whole Old Testament. ‘The Law of Moses’ is the first five books of the Bible. ‘The Prophets’ covers books such as Isaiah and Jeremiah, along with the historical books. ‘The Psalms’ stands for the third section, the writings, which begins with the Psalms. When Jesus uses all three, he is saying that the whole Old Testament is about him.

elements.passageText:
13Now that very day two of them were on their way to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. 14They were talking to each other about all the things that had happened. 15While they were talking and debating these things, Jesus himself approached and began to accompany them 16(but their eyes were kept from recognizing him). 17Then he said to them, “What are these matters you are discussing so intently as you walk along?” And they stood still, looking sad. 18Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things that have happened there in these days?” 19He said to them, “What things?” “The things concerning Jesus the Nazarene,” they replied, “a man who, with his powerful deeds and words, proved to be a prophet before God and all the people; 20and how our chief priests and leaders handed him over to be condemned to death, and crucified him. 21But we had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel. Not only this, but it is now the third day since these things happened. 22Furthermore, some women of our group amazed us. They were at the tomb early this morning, 23and when they did not find his body, they came back and said they had seen a vision of angels, who said he was alive. 24Then some of those who were with us went to the tomb, and found it just as the women had said, but they did not see him.”

25So he said to them, “You foolish people —how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! 26Wasn’t it necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and enter into his glory?” 27Then beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things written about himself in all the scriptures.

28So they approached the village where they were going. He acted as though he wanted to go farther, 29but they urged him, “Stay with us, because it is getting toward evening and the day is almost done.” So he went in to stay with them. 30When he had taken his place at the table with them, he took the bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. 31At this point their eyes were opened and they recognized him. Then he vanished out of their sight. 32They said to each other, “Didn’t our hearts burn within us while he was speaking with us on the road, while he was explaining the scriptures to us?” 33So they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem. They found the eleven and those with them gathered together 34and saying, “The Lord has really risen, and has appeared to Simon!” 35Then they told what had happened on the road, and how they recognized him when he broke the bread.

elements.question: What do the two travellers tell the stranger about Jesus (verses 17–24)? What is their disappointment?
elements.questionHint: Notice the words ‘we had hoped’ in verse 21.
elements.sampleAnswer: The pair on the road describe Jesus as a mighty prophet who was condemned by the leaders and executed on a cross. They sadly admit they had hoped he would be the one to rescue Israel. Now, three days on, women from their group have reported an empty tomb and a vision of angels saying he lives, but no one has actually seen him.
elements.mainPoint: The cross looked like **the end of their hopes**, but it was part of God’s plan.

elements.question: How does Jesus correct them, and what does he show them in the Scriptures (verses 25–27)?
elements.questionHint: Notice the word ‘necessary’ in verse 26.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus scolds them for being so slow to take in what the prophets said. He points out that the Christ had to suffer before entering his glory. Then, starting from Moses and working through all the prophets, he explains how every part of Scripture speaks about him. Suffering followed by glory is the pattern God planned.
elements.mainPoint: The Christ **had to suffer before entering his glory**, and all the Scriptures speak of him.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Jesus says all the Scriptures speak about him. Which passage from the Old Testament study would you point to first, and why?

elements.question: How do the travellers recognise Jesus (verses 28–35)? How do they react?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Jesus does at the table, and at what they say to each other.
elements.sampleAnswer: At the table Jesus takes the bread, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to them. Their eyes are opened and they recognise him, and then he vanishes out of their sight. They say that their hearts were burning within them as he spoke on the road and explained the scriptures. They get up that very hour and return to Jerusalem to tell the eleven and those with them what has happened.
elements.mainPoint: The risen Jesus **opens the Scriptures and is known** as he breaks bread.

elements.passageText:
36While they were saying these things, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.” 37But they were startled and terrified, thinking they saw a ghost. 38Then he said to them, “Why are you frightened, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? 39Look at my hands and my feet; it’s me! Touch me and see; a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have.” 40When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. 41And while they still could not believe it (because of their joy) and were amazed, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” 42So they gave him a piece of broiled fish, 43and he took it and ate it in front of them.

44Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled.” 45Then he opened their minds so they could understand the scriptures, 46and said to them, “Thus it stands written that the Christ would suffer and would rise from the dead on the third day, 47and repentance for the forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. 48You are witnesses of these things. 49And look, I am sending you what my Father promised. But stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.”

elements.question: How does Jesus show the disciples that he is truly alive (verses 36–43)?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Jesus invites them to do, and what he does himself.
elements.sampleAnswer: The group panics and thinks a ghost has walked in. Jesus calms them by showing his hands and feet, and asks them to touch him, because a ghost has no flesh and bones. To prove the point further, he asks for food and eats some fish while they watch. He is really, physically alive.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **truly and bodily alive**.

elements.question: What does Jesus say the Scriptures are about in verses 44–47, and what are the disciples to do?
elements.questionHint: Look at the three parts of the Old Testament Jesus names, and the three things written about the Christ.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells his friends that the whole Old Testament, the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, had to be fulfilled about him. He then makes them able to grasp it: the Christ would suffer and rise on the third day. After that, a message of repentance and forgiveness would go out to every nation, with Jerusalem as the starting point. They are to be his witnesses.
elements.mainPoint: **The whole Old Testament is about Christ**: his suffering, his rising and forgiveness preached to all nations.

elements.question: The travellers’ hearts burned as Jesus opened the Scriptures. When has reading the Bible made Christ real to you?
‘We had hoped…’ Where do your hopes not fit what God seems to be doing? How might seeing the whole story change that?

elements.text:
Luke 24 gives the key to the whole Bible: from Moses to the Psalms, it is about the Christ who suffers and rises, and the forgiveness that is preached to all nations. If the Old Testament studies left you with open questions, this is where many of them find their answer. Next session we see what happens when the risen King gives his Spirit.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.

chapters.chapterTitle: The Spirit and the new people

elements.text: Where we are in the story: The King has died and risen. Now he has returned to his Father, and his followers wait. This session the Spirit is given, and a new people of God is born.

elements.question: What makes a group of people attractive to outsiders? What puts outsiders off?

elements.text:
Since last time: For forty days after the resurrection, Jesus appeared to his followers and taught them about the kingdom of God. Then he told them to wait in Jerusalem for the gift his Father had promised, and was taken up into heaven before their eyes. About a hundred and twenty believers waited and prayed. Fifty days after Passover, at the Jewish festival of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came on them with a sound like a rushing wind, and they began to speak in other languages. The crowds gathered to find out what was happening, and Peter stood up to explain.

Our passage begins in the middle of Peter’s sermon.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Acts 1:1–11 (Jesus’ last words and his ascension) and Acts 2:1–21 (the day of Pentecost, and the first part of Peter’s sermon, with its quotation from the prophet Joel).

Acts 1:1–11 (NET)

1I wrote the former account, Theophilus, about all that Jesus began to do and teach 2until the day he was taken up to heaven, after he had given orders by the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. 3To the same apostles also, after his suffering, he presented himself alive with many convincing proofs. He was seen by them over a forty-day period and spoke about matters concerning the kingdom of God. 4While he was with them, he declared, “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait there for what my Father promised, which you heard about from me. 5For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

6So when they had gathered together, they began to ask him, “Lord, is this the time when you are restoring the kingdom to Israel?” 7He told them, “You are not permitted to know the times or periods that the Father has set by his own authority. 8But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the farthest parts of the earth.” 9After he had said this, while they were watching, he was lifted up and a cloud hid him from their sight. 10As they were still staring into the sky while he was going, suddenly two men in white clothing stood near them 11and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking up into the sky? This same Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come back in the same way you saw him go into heaven.”

Acts 2:1–21 (NET)

1Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place. 2Suddenly a sound like a violent wind blowing came from heaven and filled the entire house where they were sitting. 3And tongues spreading out like a fire appeared to them and came to rest on each one of them. 4All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them.

5Now there were devout Jews from every nation under heaven residing in Jerusalem. 6When this sound occurred, a crowd gathered and was in confusion, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. 7Completely baffled, they said, “Aren’t all these who are speaking Galileans? 8And how is it that each one of us hears them in our own native language? 9Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and the province of Asia, 10Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, 11both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own languages about the great deeds God has done!” 12All were astounded and greatly confused, saying to one another, “What does this mean?”

13But others jeered at the speakers, saying, “They are drunk on new wine!”

14But Peter stood up with the eleven, raised his voice, and addressed them: “You men of Judea and all you who live in Jerusalem, know this and listen carefully to what I say. 15In spite of what you think, these men are not drunk, for it is only nine o’clock in the morning. 16But this is what was spoken about through the prophet Joel: 17‘And in the last days it will be,’ God says, ‘that I will pour out my Spirit on all people, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy, and your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams. 18Even on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy. 19And I will perform wonders in the sky above and miraculous signs on the earth below, blood and fire and clouds of smoke. 20The sun will be changed to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. 21And then everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

elements.passageText:
22“Men of Israel, listen to these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man clearly attested to you by God with powerful deeds, wonders, and miraculous signs that God performed among you through him, just as you yourselves know— 23this man, who was handed over by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you executed by nailing him to a cross at the hands of Gentiles. 24But God raised him up, having released him from the pains of death, because it was not possible for him to be held in its power.

25For David says about him, ‘I saw the Lord always in front of me, for he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken. 26Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced; my body also will live in hope, 27because you will not leave my soul in Hades, nor permit your Holy One to experience decay. 28You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of joy with your presence.’ 29“Brothers, I can speak confidently to you about our forefather David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. 30So then, because he was a prophet and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath to seat one of his descendants on his throne, 31David by foreseeing this spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was neither abandoned to Hades, nor did his body experience decay.

32This Jesus God raised up, and we are all witnesses of it. 33So then, exalted to the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out what you both see and hear. 34For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my lord, “Sit at my right hand 35until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’ 36Therefore let all the house of Israel know beyond a doubt that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ.”

elements.question: What does Peter say about Jesus’ life and death, and what did God do (verses 22–24)?
elements.questionHint: Look at who did what: the people, and God.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter reminds his audience that Jesus showed by miraculous signs that God was with him. Jesus was then handed over, as part of God’s settled plan, and nailed to a cross through the hands of lawless people. God overturned that verdict by raising him from death, since death could never keep him. His death was both a human crime and God’s purpose.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus’ death was both a human crime and **God’s plan**, and God **raised him up**.

elements.question: How does Peter use David’s words in verses 25–35 to show that Jesus is the promised king?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Peter says David did, and what God had promised him.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter argues that David could not have been writing about himself, since David died, was buried and has a tomb that is still known. David was a prophet who knew that God had promised on oath that one of his descendants would reign. So David was really looking ahead to the Christ being raised from the dead. Jesus has been lifted to God’s right hand, and from there has sent the Spirit.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus is the promised king**, raised by God, who has poured out the Spirit.

elements.question: What conclusion does Peter draw in verse 36, and who is it addressed to?
elements.questionHint: Notice the two titles, and the word ‘whole’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter ends with a challenge to all Israel: they can be certain that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ. The very man they put on a cross is now the ruler and the promised king. The rejected one is vindicated.
elements.mainPoint: God has made the crucified Jesus **both Lord and Christ**.

elements.passageText:
37Now when they heard this, they were acutely distressed and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “What should we do, brothers?” 38Peter said to them, “Repent, and each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 39For the promise is for you and your children, and for all who are far away, as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” 40With many other words he testified and exhorted them saying, “Save yourselves from this perverse generation!” 41So those who accepted his message were baptized, and that day about 3,000 people were added.

42They were devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. 43Reverential awe came over everyone, and many wonders and miraculous signs came about by the apostles. 44All who believed were together and held everything in common, 45and they began selling their property and possessions and distributing the proceeds to everyone, as anyone had need. 46Every day they continued to gather together by common consent in the temple courts, breaking bread from house to house, sharing their food with glad and humble hearts, 47praising God and having the good will of all the people. And the Lord was adding to their number every day those who were being saved.

elements.question: How do the crowds respond, and what does Peter tell them to do and promise them (verses 37–41)?
elements.questionHint: Look for the two commands and the two promises in verses 38–39.
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter’s words shake the audience, who ask, ‘What should we do?’ His answer: repent, be baptised in Jesus’ name to have their sins forgiven, and receive the Holy Spirit as a gift. This offer extends to them, their children and even people far off, whoever the Lord chooses. Roughly three thousand join them that day.
elements.mainPoint: The way in is to **repent and receive Jesus**: forgiveness and the Spirit are promised to all whom God calls.
keyTerms: acutely distressed|distressed|cut to the heart|what should we do|what shall we do

elements.question: What marks the life of the new community in verses 42–47?
elements.questionHint: Look at what they devote themselves to, and at what they do with their possessions.
elements.sampleAnswer: The believers are committed to four things: the teaching of the apostles, shared life, sharing meals together and praying. They are generous, sharing what they own so that nobody lacks. Day after day they gather in the temple area and in homes, praising God, and the Lord keeps adding people who are being saved.
elements.mainPoint: The new community is **built around the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer**.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Compare this community with Israel at Sinai (Old Testament session 4). What is similar, and what is new?

elements.question: Who are God’s people in this passage, where do they gather, and who is their King?
elements.questionHint: Think about people, place and rule.
elements.sampleAnswer: God’s people are those who repent, are baptised and believe, whatever their background, and thousands are added to them. They gather in the temple courts and in one another’s homes, so the place is no longer a territory but the community itself. Their King is Jesus, whom God has made Lord and Christ and who reigns at God’s right hand. The kingdom pattern has been renewed around him.
elements.mainPoint: God’s people are **those who turn to Jesus** (people), gathered in **the temple courts and in homes** (place), around **Jesus as Lord and Christ** (rule).

elements.question: The promise is ‘for you and your children, and for all who are far away’. What does it mean to you that you are included?
Which mark of the early church (teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer, generosity) most needs strengthening in your own church? What could you do about it?

elements.text:
The Spirit’s coming makes the kingdom visible in a new way: a people gathered around the risen King, who share his life. The promise of the new covenant, with its changed hearts and forgiven sin, is beginning to come true. Next session we see how Paul explains the basis for this forgiveness.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: A new people is forming, forgiven and filled with the Spirit. This session Paul explains how God can forgive sinners and still be just.

elements.question: Imagine a guilty person being declared not guilty in a court of law. How would that person feel, and what would it cost someone?

elements.text:
Since last time: Acts tells how the good news travelled from Jerusalem to the nations. Saul, once a persecutor, was met by the risen Christ and became Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles. He planted churches across the Roman world and wrote letters to them. Romans, probably written around AD 57, is the fullest of those letters, and was written to a church he had not yet visited.

In the early chapters of Romans Paul argues that everyone, Jew and Gentile alike, is guilty before God and cannot save themselves. Our passage begins where that argument ends.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Romans 3:9–20 (the verdict on all people), and Romans 4 (how Abraham was put right with God by faith, which echoes Genesis 15 in the Old Testament study).

Romans 3:9–20 (NET)

9What then? Are we better off? Certainly not, for we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, 10just as it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one, 11there is no one who understands, there is no one who seeks God. 12All have turned away, together they have become worthless; there is no one who shows kindness, not even one.” 13“Their throats are open graves, they deceive with their tongues, the poison of asps is under their lips.” 14“Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.” 15“Their feet are swift to shed blood, 16ruin and misery are in their paths,

17and the way of peace they have not known.” 18“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

19Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world may be held accountable to God. 20For no one is declared righteous before him by the works of the law, for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.

Romans 4 (NET)

1What then shall we say that Abraham, our ancestor according to the flesh, has discovered regarding this matter? 2For if Abraham was declared righteous by works, he has something to boast about—but not before God. 3For what does the scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” 4Now to the one who works, his pay is not credited due to grace but due to obligation. 5But to the one who does not work, but believes in the one who declares the ungodly righteous, his faith is credited as righteousness.

6So even David himself speaks regarding the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: 7“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; 8blessed is the one against whom the Lord will never count sin.”

9Is this blessedness then for the circumcision or also for the uncircumcision? For we say, “faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness.” 10How then was it credited to him? Was he circumcised at the time, or not? No, he was not circumcised but uncircumcised! 11And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised, so that he would become the father of all those who believe but have never been circumcised, that they too could have righteousness credited to them. 12And he is also the father of the circumcised, who are not only circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham possessed when he was still uncircumcised.

13For the promise to Abraham or to his descendants that he would inherit the world was not fulfilled through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith. 14For if they become heirs by the law, faith is empty and the promise is nullified. 15For the law brings wrath, because where there is no law there is no transgression either. 16For this reason it is by faith so that it may be by grace, with the result that the promise may be certain to all the descendants—not only to those who are under the law, but also to those who have the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all 17(as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations”). He is our father in the presence of God whom he believed—the God who makes the dead alive and summons the things that do not yet exist as though they already do. 18Against hope Abraham believed in hope with the result that he became the father of many nations according to the pronouncement, “so will your descendants be.” 19Without being weak in faith, he considered his own body as dead (because he was about 100 years old) and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. 20He did not waver in unbelief about the promise of God but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God.

21He was fully convinced that what God promised he was also able to do. 22So indeed it was credited to Abraham as righteousness.

23But the statement it was credited to him was not written only for Abraham’s sake, 24but also for our sake, to whom it will be credited, those who believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. 25He was given over because of our transgressions and was raised for the sake of our justification.

elements.question: Tap to see what ‘justified’ means.
elements.answer: To be ‘justified’ is to be declared righteous: God, as judge, announces that a sinner is in the right with him. It is a legal word, not a description of how good someone has become. Paul says it is given freely, on the basis of what Christ has done, and received by faith.

elements.passageText: 21But now apart from the law the righteousness of God (although it is attested by the law and the prophets) has been disclosed— 22namely, the righteousness of God through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction, 23for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. 24But they are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. 25God publicly displayed him at his death as the mercy seat accessible through faith. This was to demonstrate his righteousness, because God in his forbearance had passed over the sins previously committed. 26This was also to demonstrate his righteousness in the present time, so that he would be just and the justifier of the one who lives because of Jesus’ faithfulness.

elements.question: How does Paul say people are put right with God, and who is it for (verses 21–22)?
elements.questionHint: Notice the phrases ‘apart from the law’ and ‘no distinction’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says that the righteousness of God, his way of putting people right, is now plain. It does not depend on keeping the law, though the Old Testament pointed to it. It comes through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, and it is for everyone who trusts. Nobody is in a different position, because all are in the same situation.
elements.mainPoint: Righteousness comes **through faith in Christ, not through the law**, for everyone who believes.

elements.question: What does Paul say about the human condition and about what Jesus has done (verses 23–25)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the three words in verses 24–25: justified, redemption and mercy seat.
elements.sampleAnswer: Everyone has sinned and falls short of God’s glory. Even so, they can be justified freely as God’s gift of grace, through the redemption that Christ Jesus achieved, a price paid to set them free. God openly set Jesus before the world at his death as the mercy seat, a place where sin is dealt with, reached through faith.
elements.mainPoint: All have sinned, yet all can be **justified freely** through Christ, displayed at his death as the mercy seat.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Redemption is a word from the slave market, and ‘mercy seat’ from the temple. What does each picture add to your understanding?

elements.question: Why did God put Jesus forward in this way (verses 25–26)? What does it show about God?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Paul says about God’s righteousness and his patience.
elements.sampleAnswer: God’s purpose was to show that he is righteous. In his patience he had let earlier sins go unpunished, which could make him look unjust. Now, in Christ, his justice is made plain, so that he is just himself and also the one who justifies anyone who relies on Jesus. He neither ignores sin nor refuses to forgive it.
elements.mainPoint: At the cross God shows that he is **both just and the one who justifies**.

elements.passageText:
1Therefore, since we have been declared righteous by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2through whom we have also obtained access into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in the hope of God’s glory. 3Not only this, but we also rejoice in sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, 4and endurance, character, and character, hope. 5And hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.

6For while we were still helpless, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. 7(For rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person perhaps someone might possibly dare to die.) 8But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

9Much more then, because we have now been declared righteous by his blood, we will be saved through him from God’s wrath. 10For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, how much more, since we have been reconciled, will we be saved by his life? 11Not only this, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received this reconciliation.

elements.question: What do believers have because they have been justified by faith (verses 1–2)?
elements.questionHint: Look for three things that Christ has given us.
elements.sampleAnswer: Because God has declared believers righteous, they now enjoy peace with him through their Lord Jesus Christ. Faith has opened a door into the favour in which they stand firm. They celebrate the hope of sharing God’s glory. Their position is safe, as it depends on Christ’s work and not on theirs.
elements.mainPoint: Those declared righteous have **peace with God** and a secure hope.

elements.question: How does Paul show how great God’s love is in verses 6–8?
elements.questionHint: Notice who Christ died for, and when.
elements.sampleAnswer: At just the right moment Christ died on behalf of people who were powerless and had no time for God. Hardly anyone would give their life for a righteous person, though for someone truly good a person might risk it. Yet God proves his love in this way: Christ died for us when we were still sinners, so love came before any merit on our part.
elements.mainPoint: God’s love is proved because **Christ died for us while we were still sinners**.

elements.question: What are the results of Christ’s death for those who believe, according to verses 9–11?
elements.questionHint: Look at the contrast between ‘enemies’ and ‘reconciled’, and between wrath and being saved.
elements.sampleAnswer: Having been declared righteous by Christ’s blood, believers will be saved from God’s wrath. They were once his enemies but were reconciled to him by the death of his Son, and his risen life will now save them completely. This makes them rejoice in God, through Jesus, who has brought the restored relationship.
elements.mainPoint: Believers are **saved from wrath and reconciled to God**, and so they rejoice.

elements.question: Paul says Christ died for us ‘while we were still sinners’. What difference does it make that God’s love came before we deserved it?
Paul lists peace, access and hope. Which of these do you most need to hold onto this week, and why?

elements.text:
The Old Testament’s deepest question was how sinners could be forgiven by a holy God. Paul’s answer is that God himself provided what was needed in Christ. The servant of Isaiah 53 has borne sin, and the new covenant’s forgiveness has a firm basis. Next session we see the effect on the shape of God’s people.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: Sinners are forgiven and justified in Christ. This session Paul shows what that means for the people of God: one family made of those who were once far apart.

elements.question: What divides people in your community? How do those divisions show up in church?

elements.text:
Since last time: As the gospel spread, non-Jews (Gentiles) came to faith in large numbers. This raised a big question: did they have to become Jewish to belong to God’s people? The apostles decided that they did not (Acts 15), and Paul wrote letters to explain why. Ephesians was written while Paul was in prison, to churches in what is now western Turkey.

In the first half of Ephesians Paul praises God for the blessings given in Christ, and says that those who were dead in sin have been saved by grace through faith (Ephesians 1–2:10). Our passage turns to what that means for Jews and Gentiles together.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Ephesians 1:3–14 (the blessings God gives in Christ) and Ephesians 2:1–10 (saved by grace through faith), which lead straight into today’s passage.

Ephesians 1:3–14 (NET)

3Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in Christ. 4For he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. 5He did this by predestining us to adoption as his legal heirs through Jesus Christ, according to the pleasure of his will— 6to the praise of the glory of his grace that he has freely bestowed on us in his dearly loved Son. 7In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our offenses, according to the riches of his grace 8that he lavished on us in all wisdom and insight. 9He did this when he revealed to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure that he set forth in Christ, 10toward the administration of the fullness of the times, to head up all things in Christ—the things in heaven and the things on earth.

11In Christ we too have been claimed as God’s own possession, since we were predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will 12so that we, who were the first to set our hope on Christ, would be to the praise of his glory. 13And when you heard the word of truth (the gospel of your salvation)—when you believed in Christ —you were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit, 14who is the down payment of our inheritance, until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.

Ephesians 2:1–10 (NET)

1And although you were dead in your offenses and sins, 2in which you formerly lived according to this world’s present path, according to the ruler of the domain of the air, the ruler of the spirit that is now energizing the sons of disobedience, 3among whom all of us also formerly lived out our lives in the cravings of our flesh, indulging the desires of the flesh and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath even as the rest…

4But God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, 5even though we were dead in offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you are saved! — 6and he raised us up together with him and seated us together with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, 7to demonstrate in the coming ages the surpassing wealth of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. 8For by grace you are saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God; 9it is not from works, so that no one can boast. 10For we are his creative work, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we can do them.

elements.passageText:
11Therefore remember that formerly you, the Gentiles in the flesh—who are called “uncircumcision” by the so-called “circumcision” that is performed on the body by human hands— 12that you were at that time without the Messiah, alienated from the citizenship of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. 13But now in Christ Jesus you who used to be far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

14For he is our peace, the one who made both groups into one and who destroyed the middle wall of partition, the hostility, 15when he nullified in his flesh the law of commandments in decrees. He did this to create in himself one new man out of two, thus making peace, 16and to reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, by which the hostility has been killed. 17And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near, 18so that through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

19So then you are no longer foreigners and noncitizens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, 20because you have been built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. 21In him the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, 22in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.

elements.question: How does Paul describe the situation of the Gentiles before Christ (verses 11–12)?
elements.questionHint: Make a list of what they lacked.
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says Gentile believers once had no Messiah, were excluded from Israel’s citizenship, and were strangers to the covenants of promise. That left them without hope and without God in the world. They stood outside everything God had promised his people.
elements.mainPoint: Without Christ, Gentiles were **outsiders to God’s promises** and without hope.

elements.question: What has Christ done to bring distant people near (verses 13–16)? What has he done about the hostility between Jew and Gentile?
elements.questionHint: Look for how Paul describes the barrier, and what happened to it.
elements.sampleAnswer: Christ’s death on the cross has made the far-off ones near, since his blood paid the price. He is the peace between Jews and Gentiles, having demolished the barrier of hostility separating them. In place of two groups, he formed a single new humanity, and through the cross he reconciled both to God.
elements.mainPoint: By his cross **Christ has made one new people** of Jew and Gentile, and reconciled them to God.

elements.question: How do both groups now come to God (verses 17–18)?
elements.questionHint: Look at who preached peace and who is involved in the ‘access’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Christ proclaimed peace to people far from God and to people near him. So both Jews and Gentiles now reach the Father by the same route: through him, in one Spirit. Neither group has an advantage.
elements.mainPoint: Jew and Gentile now come **to the Father together**, through Christ, by one Spirit.

elements.question: What new pictures does Paul use for the people of God in verses 19–22?
elements.questionHint: Look for a nation, a family and a building.
elements.sampleAnswer: Gentile believers are no longer outsiders. They are fellow citizens with God’s people and part of his family. The apostles’ and prophets’ teaching is the base they are built on, with Jesus as the cornerstone. Together they are becoming a holy temple, a home for God through his Spirit.
elements.mainPoint: The people of God are **a family and a temple**, built on Christ, where God lives by his Spirit.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: In the Old Testament God’s presence was in the tabernacle and the temple. What is different about where God lives in verses 21–22?

elements.question: How do people, place and rule appear in this passage?
elements.questionHint: Think about the new humanity, the new temple and the cornerstone.
elements.sampleAnswer: The people are one new humanity, Jews and Gentiles together, God’s household and fellow citizens. The place is a new temple: God’s dwelling is no longer a building but his people, in whom he lives by the Spirit. The rule is Christ’s: he is the cornerstone, the peace between them, and the one through whom they have access to the Father. The kingdom pattern has been reshaped around Christ.
elements.mainPoint: In Christ **people, place and rule are renewed**: **one new humanity** (people), **God’s temple in his people** (place) and **Christ the cornerstone** (rule).

elements.question: Where do ethnic, tribal, social or denominational walls still stand in your church or community? What would it look like to treat them as already torn down in Christ?
You are being built into a dwelling place for God. How does that change the way you think about meeting with other Christians?

elements.text:
The Old Testament promised blessing for all nations through Abraham’s family. Here the promise is coming true: one family, made up of those once near and those once far, united by the cross. The people of God are being formed. Next session we look at how the whole system of priests and sacrifices finds its fulfilment.

Where we are in the story: God’s people are one family, forgiven in Christ. This session we see how Jesus completes everything the temple, the priests and the sacrifices pointed to.
