elements.text:
Since last time: Hebrews is a sermon-like letter written to Jewish Christians who were under pressure and tempted to go back to their old ways of worship. The writer argues that this would be a step backwards, because Jesus is better than everything that came before. In chapters 1–7 he shows that Jesus is greater than the angels, greater than Moses, and a better priest than any who served in the temple, in the order of Melchizedek.

Our passage takes up the heart of the argument: the new covenant, and the sacrifice that makes it work.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Hebrews 1:1–4 (God has spoken finally in his Son), Hebrews 4:14–5:10 (Jesus the great high priest) and Hebrews 7:23–28 (a priest for ever). For the background to the temple’s great day, read Leviticus 16 (the Day of Atonement).

Hebrews 1:1–4 (NET)

1After God spoke long ago in various portions and in various ways to our ancestors through the prophets, 2in these last days he has spoken to us in a son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom he created the world. 3The Son is the radiance of his glory and the representation of his essence, and he sustains all things by his powerful word, and so when he had accomplished cleansing for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. 4Thus he became so far better than the angels as he has inherited a name superior to theirs.

Hebrews 4:14–5:10 (NET)

14Therefore since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession. 15For we do not have a high priest incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin. 16Therefore let us confidently approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace whenever we need help.

5:1For every high priest is taken from among the people and appointed to represent them before God, to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. 2He is able to deal compassionately with those who are ignorant and erring, since he also is subject to weakness, 3and for this reason he is obligated to make sin offerings for himself as well as for the people. 4And no one assumes this honor on his own initiative, but only when called to it by God, as in fact Aaron was. 5So also Christ did not glorify himself in becoming high priest, but the one who glorified him was God, who said to him, “You are my Son! Today I have fathered you,” 6as also in another place God says, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” 7During his earthly life Christ offered both requests and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death and he was heard because of his devotion. 8Although he was a son, he learned obedience through the things he suffered.

9And by being perfected in this way, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, 10and he was designated by God as high priest in the order of Melchizedek.

Hebrews 7:23–28 (NET)

23And the others who became priests were numerous, because death prevented them from continuing in office, 24but he holds his priesthood permanently since he lives forever. 25So he is able to save completely those who come to God through him, because he always lives to intercede for them. 26For it is indeed fitting for us to have such a high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separate from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. 27He has no need to do every day what those priests do, to offer sacrifices first for their own sins and then for the sins of the people, since he did this in offering himself once for all. 28For the law appoints as high priests men subject to weakness, but the word of solemn affirmation that came after the law appoints a son made perfect forever.

Leviticus 16 (NET)

1The [[sc:Lord]] spoke to Moses after the death of Aaron’s two sons when they approached the presence of the [[sc:Lord]] and died, 2and the [[sc:Lord]] said to Moses: “Tell Aaron your brother that he must not enter at any time into the Holy Place inside the special curtain in front of the atonement lid that is on the ark so that he may not die, for I will appear in the cloud over the atonement lid.

3“In this way Aaron is to enter into the sanctuary—with a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering. 4He must put on a holy linen tunic, linen leggings are to cover his body, and he is to wrap himself with a linen sash and wrap his head with a linen turban. They are holy garments, so he must bathe his body in water and put them on. 5He must also take two male goats from the congregation of the Israelites for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering. 6Then Aaron is to present the sin offering bull which is for himself and is to make atonement on behalf of himself and his household. 7Next he must take the two goats and stand them before the [[sc:Lord]] at the entrance of the Meeting Tent, 8and Aaron is to cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the [[sc:Lord]] and one lot for Azazel. 9Aaron must then present the goat which has been designated by lot for the [[sc:Lord]], and he is to make it a sin offering, 10but the goat which has been designated by lot for Azazel is to be stood alive before the [[sc:Lord]] to make atonement on it by sending it away into the desert to Azazel.

11“Aaron is to present the sin-offering bull which is for himself, and he is to make atonement on behalf of himself and his household. He is to slaughter the sin-offering bull which is for himself, 12and take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar before the [[sc:Lord]] and a full double handful of finely ground fragrant incense, and bring them inside the curtain. 13He must then put the incense on the fire before the [[sc:Lord]], and the cloud of incense will cover the atonement lid which is above the ark of the testimony, so that he will not die. 14Then he is to take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger on the eastern face of the atonement lid, and in front of the atonement lid he is to sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger.

15“Aaron must then slaughter the sin-offering goat which is for the people. He is to bring its blood inside the curtain, and he is to do with its blood just as he did to the blood of the bull: He is to sprinkle it on the atonement lid and in front of the atonement lid. 16So he is to make atonement for the Holy Place from the impurities of the Israelites and from their transgressions with regard to all their sins, and thus he is to do for the Meeting Tent which resides with them in the midst of their impurities. 17Nobody is to be in the Meeting Tent when he enters to make atonement in the Holy Place until he goes out, and he has made atonement on his behalf, on behalf of his household, and on behalf of the whole assembly of Israel.

18“Then Aaron is to go out to the altar which is before the [[sc:Lord]] and make atonement for it. He is to take some of the blood of the bull and some of the blood of the goat, and put it all around on the horns of the altar. 19Then he is to sprinkle on it some of the blood with his finger seven times, and cleanse and consecrate it from the impurities of the Israelites.

20“When Aaron has finished purifying the Holy Place, the Meeting Tent, and the altar, he is to present the live goat. 21Aaron is to lay his two hands on the head of the live goat and confess over it all the iniquities of the Israelites and all their transgressions in regard to all their sins, and thus he is to put them on the head of the goat and send it away into the desert by the hand of a man standing ready. 22The goat is to bear on itself all their iniquities into an inaccessible land, so he is to send the goat away into the desert.

23“Aaron must then enter the Meeting Tent and take off the linen garments which he had put on when he entered the sanctuary, and leave them there. 24Then he must bathe his body in water in the Holy Place, put on his clothes, and go out and make his burnt offering and the people’s burnt offering. So he is to make atonement on behalf of himself and the people.

25“Then he is to offer up the fat of the sin offering in smoke on the altar, 26and the one who sent the goat away to Azazel must wash his clothes, bathe his body in water, and afterward he may reenter the camp. 27The bull of the sin offering and the goat of the sin offering, whose blood was brought to make atonement in the Holy Place, must be brought outside the camp and their hide, their flesh, and their dung must be burned up, 28and the one who burns them must wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may reenter the camp.

29“This is to be a perpetual statute for you. In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you must humble yourselves and do no work of any kind, both the native citizen and the resident foreigner who lives in your midst, 30for on this day atonement is to be made for you to cleanse you from all your sins; you must be clean before the [[sc:Lord]]. 31It is to be a Sabbath of complete rest for you, and you must humble yourselves. It is a perpetual statute.

32“The priest who is anointed and ordained to act as high priest in place of his father is to make atonement. He is to put on the linen garments, the holy garments, 33and he is to purify the Most Holy Place, he is to purify the Meeting Tent and the altar, and he is to make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly. 34This is to be a perpetual statute for you to make atonement for the Israelites for all their sins once a year.” So he did just as the [[sc:Lord]] had commanded Moses.

elements.question: Tap to see what a high priest did.
elements.answer: In the Old Testament the high priest was the one man who could enter the most holy place in the tabernacle or temple, once a year, on the Day of Atonement. He brought the blood of a sacrifice, first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. Hebrews says that Jesus is the true and final high priest.

elements.passageText:
1Now the main point of what we are saying is this: We have such a high priest, one who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, 2a minister in the sanctuary and the true tabernacle that the Lord, not man, set up. 3For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices. So this one too had to have something to offer. 4Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are already priests who offer the gifts prescribed by the law. 5The place where they serve is a sketch and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary, just as Moses was warned by God as he was about to complete the tabernacle. For he says, “See that you make everything according to the design shown to you on the mountain.” 6But now Jesus has obtained a superior ministry, since the covenant that he mediates is also better and is enacted on better promises.

7For if that first covenant had been faultless, no one would have looked for a second one. 8But showing its fault, God says to them, “Look, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. 9“It will not be like the covenant that I made with their fathers, on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, because they did not continue in my covenant and I had no regard for them, says the Lord. 10“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord. I will put my laws in their minds and I will inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God and they will be my people. 11“And there will be no need at all for each one to teach his countryman or each one to teach his brother saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ since they will all know me, from the least to the greatest. 12“For I will be merciful toward their evil deeds, and their sins I will remember no longer.” 13When he speaks of a new covenant, he makes the first obsolete. Now what is growing obsolete and aging is about to disappear.

elements.question: Where is Jesus serving as high priest, and why is his ministry better than the earthly priests’ (verses 1–6)?
elements.questionHint: Look at where he is seated, and what the earthly priests serve.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus has taken the place of highest honour, at God’s right hand, and serves in the genuine heavenly sanctuary that God, not people, put up. Earthly priests labour in a mere shadow of that reality. His work is far superior, because he mediates a better covenant resting on better promises.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus serves in **heaven itself**, as mediator of a better covenant.

elements.question: What fault does the writer find in the first covenant, and what does he say God promised (verses 7–9)?
elements.questionHint: Notice whom God finds fault with.
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer reasons that a perfect first covenant would not have needed a successor. The trouble lay with the people, who did not continue in it, and God said so. That is why God spoke of days coming when he would make a new covenant with Israel and Judah.
elements.mainPoint: **The people failed** under the first covenant, so God promised a new one.
keyTerms: did not continue|brok|did not remain|did not keep

elements.question: Which promises from the new covenant are quoted in verses 10–12? Compare them with Jeremiah 31 in the Old Testament study.
elements.questionHint: Count the promises God makes beginning ‘I will’.
elements.sampleAnswer: God pledges to place his laws in people’s minds and fix them on their hearts. He will be their God and they will be his people. Everyone, from the lowest to the highest, will know him, and he will show mercy towards their wrongdoing and forget their sins. The writer is quoting Jeremiah’s promise and says it has now arrived.
elements.mainPoint: The **new covenant** of Jeremiah 31 has arrived: God’s law on the heart, and sins forgiven.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The writer says that calling the covenant ‘new’ makes the first one obsolete (verse 13). What do you think he means, and what does he not mean?

elements.passageText: 11But now Christ has come as the high priest of the good things to come. He passed through the greater and more perfect tent not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, 12and he entered once for all into the Most Holy Place not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, and so he himself secured eternal redemption. 13For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a young cow sprinkled on those who are defiled consecrated them and provided ritual purity, 14how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our consciences from dead works to worship the living God.

elements.question: How is Christ’s service as high priest different from that of the earthly priests (verses 11–12)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the tent, the blood and the number of times.
elements.sampleAnswer: Christ has come as high priest and entered a better and more perfect sanctuary, one that no human built. He went in once and for all, not with the blood of animals but with his own blood. By that he secured an everlasting redemption for his people.
elements.mainPoint: Christ entered God’s presence **once for all with his own blood**, securing eternal redemption.

elements.question: How does Christ’s sacrifice compare with animal sacrifices (verses 13–14)? What does it achieve in us?
elements.questionHint: Look at what animal sacrifices could do, and what Christ’s blood can do.
elements.sampleAnswer: Animal sacrifices could do no more than make a person ritually clean on the outside. Christ, through the eternal Spirit, presented himself to God as a perfect offering without blemish, so his blood reaches the conscience, freeing us from dead works so that we can worship the living God. The cleansing is deep and inward.
elements.mainPoint: Christ’s sacrifice **cleanses the conscience**, not just the outside.
keyTerms: blood of christ|his blood|offered himself|without blemish
conscienc|consciences|cleans|purif|purifies|dead works|worship the living god|serve the living god

elements.question: Putting both passages together, what does Jesus do that the old priests and sacrifices could never do?
elements.questionHint: Think about how often, how deeply, and for how long.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus offers one sacrifice once for all, rather than many repeated ones. His blood cleanses the conscience, not just the outward person. He is the mediator of a covenant that writes God’s law on the heart and forgives sin for good. He has entered the very presence of God on behalf of his people, and his priesthood is eternal.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus does **once and for all** what the old priests and sacrifices could never do.

elements.question: Hebrews says Christ’s blood can cleanse the conscience. What do you tend to do with guilt, and what would it look like to bring it to Christ?
Jesus serves in heaven on behalf of his people. What does it mean to you that someone is there for you?

elements.text:
Hebrews shows that the covenants, the priests and the sacrifices of the Old Testament were never the final answer. They were shadows, and Christ is the reality. The new covenant Jeremiah promised is here, based on a sacrifice that does what the old ones never could. One part of the story remains: where it all leads.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: God’s people are one family, forgiven and cleansed in Christ. This last session we look at where the story ends: the kingdom completed.

elements.question: How do you think the world’s story will end? What would you most like to be true about the end?

elements.text:
Since last time: The New Testament letters from Peter, John, James and others encourage believers to stand firm, to love one another and to wait for Christ’s return. By the end of the first century the church was spread across the Roman world and often under pressure. John, an old apostle, was exiled to the island of Patmos, where the risen Christ gave him the visions recorded in Revelation.

These visions show Christ ruling, the church under pressure, and the powers of evil rising and being defeated. They are written in dramatic symbols, and they sweep through conflict and judgement to the final victory over evil. Our passage is the climax. This study moves directly from the Lamb’s victory to the new creation.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Revelation 1:9–20 (John sees the risen Christ), Revelation 5 (the Lamb who was slain) and Revelation 19:11–21 (Christ the rider on the white horse). You will meet some of the book’s symbols, and see why the Lamb is at the centre.

Revelation 1:9–20 (NET)

9I, John, your brother and the one who shares with you in the persecution, kingdom, and endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony about Jesus. 10I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day when I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet, 11saying: “Write in a book what you see and send it to the seven churches—to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

12I turned to see whose voice was speaking to me, and when I did so, I saw seven golden lampstands, 13and in the midst of the lampstands was one like a son of man. He was dressed in a robe extending down to his feet and he wore a wide golden belt around his chest. 14His head and hair were as white as wool, even as white as snow, and his eyes were like a fiery flame. 15His feet were like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and his voice was like the roar of many waters. 16He held seven stars in his right hand, and a sharp double-edged sword extended out of his mouth. His face shone like the sun shining at full strength. 17When I saw him I fell down at his feet as though I were dead, but he placed his right hand on me and said: “Do not be afraid! I am the first and the last, 18and the one who lives! I was dead, but look, now I am alive—forever and ever—and I hold the keys of death and of Hades! 19Therefore write what you saw, what is, and what will be after these things.

20The mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand and the seven golden lampstands is this: The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.

Revelation 5 (NET)

1Then I saw in the right hand of the one who was seated on the throne a scroll written on the front and back and sealed with seven seals. 2And I saw a powerful angel proclaiming in a loud voice: “Who is worthy to open the scroll and to break its seals?” 3But no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or look into it. 4So I began weeping bitterly because no one was found who was worthy to open the scroll or to look into it. 5Then one of the elders said to me, “Stop weeping! Look, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered; thus he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

6Then I saw standing in the middle of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the middle of the elders, a Lamb that appeared to have been killed. He had seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. 7Then he came and took the scroll from the right hand of the one who was seated on the throne, 8and when he had taken the scroll, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders threw themselves to the ground before the Lamb. Each of them had a harp and golden bowls full of incense (which are the prayers of the saints). 9They were singing a new song: “You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals because you were killed, and at the cost of your own blood you have purchased for God persons from every tribe, language, people, and nation. 10You have appointed them as a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign on the earth.”

11Then I looked and heard the voice of many angels in a circle around the throne, as well as the living creatures and the elders. Their number was ten thousand times ten thousand —thousands times thousands— 12all of whom were singing in a loud voice: “Worthy is the lamb who was killed to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and praise!”

13Then I heard every creature—in heaven, on earth, under the earth, in the sea, and all that is in them—singing: “To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be praise, honor, glory, and ruling power forever and ever!”

14And the four living creatures were saying “Amen,” and the elders threw themselves to the ground and worshiped.

Revelation 19:11–21 (NET)

11Then I saw heaven opened and here came a white horse! The one riding it was called “Faithful” and “True,” and with justice he judges and goes to war. 12His eyes are like a fiery flame and there are many diadem crowns on his head. He has a name written that no one knows except himself. 13He is dressed in clothing dipped in blood, and he is called the Word of God. 14The armies that are in heaven, dressed in white, clean, fine linen, were following him on white horses. 15From his mouth extends a sharp sword, so that with it he can strike the nations. He will rule them with an iron rod, and he stomps the winepress of the furious wrath of God, the All-Powerful. 16He has a name written on his clothing and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

17Then I saw one angel standing in the sun, and he shouted in a loud voice to all the birds flying high in the sky: “Come, gather around for the great banquet of God, 18to eat your fill of the flesh of kings, the flesh of generals, the flesh of powerful people, the flesh of horses and those who ride them, and the flesh of all people, both free and slave, and small and great!”

19Then I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies assembled to do battle with the one who rode the horse and with his army. 20Now the beast was seized, and along with him the false prophet who had performed the signs on his behalf —signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped his image. Both of them were thrown alive into the lake of fire burning with sulfur. 21The others were killed by the sword that extended from the mouth of the one who rode the horse, and all the birds gorged themselves with their flesh.

elements.text: A new heaven and a new earth

elements.passageText:
1Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had ceased to exist, and the sea existed no more. 2And I saw the holy city—the new Jerusalem—descending out of heaven from God, made ready like a bride adorned for her husband. 3And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Look! The residence of God is among human beings. He will live among them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. 4He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will not exist any more—or mourning, or crying, or pain, for the former things have ceased to exist.”

5And the one seated on the throne said: “Look! I am making all things new!” Then he said to me, “Write it down, because these words are reliable and true.” 6He also said to me, “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. To the one who is thirsty I will give water free of charge from the spring of the water of life. 7The one who conquers will inherit these things, and I will be his God and he will be my son. 8But as for the cowards, unbelievers, detestable persons, murderers, the sexually immoral, and those who practice magic spells, idol worshipers, and all those who lie, their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. That is the second death.”

elements.question: What does John see, and what is the central promise he hears in verse 3?
elements.questionHint: Listen to the loud voice from the throne.
elements.sampleAnswer: John sees a brand-new heaven and earth, since the old ones are gone, and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God dressed like a bride. A loud voice declares that God’s home is now among people. He will live with them, and they will be his people, with God himself present.
elements.mainPoint: **God will live with his people** in a new heaven and earth.

elements.question: What does God remove in verse 4, and what does the statement ‘the former things have ceased to exist’ tell you?
elements.questionHint: List what will no longer be.
elements.sampleAnswer: God will personally comfort his people, removing every tear. Death will be abolished, along with grief, crying and pain. All of this belonged to the old order, which has ceased to exist, so the effects of the fall are reversed.
elements.mainPoint: God **removes all that sin brought**: tears, death, mourning and pain.

elements.question: Who speaks in verses 5–8? What does he say about himself? What does he promise to those who are thirsty and to those who conquer?
elements.questionHint: Notice the speaker’s two sets of titles and the two promises.
elements.sampleAnswer: The speaker on the throne says that he is making everything new, and describes himself as Alpha and Omega, the start and the finish. Anyone who is thirsty may drink from the spring of life’s water free of charge. The person who overcomes will inherit all this, with God as his God and himself as God’s child.
elements.mainPoint: The One on the throne **makes everything new**, and gives life freely to the thirsty.

elements.passageText:
1Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life—water as clear as crystal—pouring out from the throne of God and of the Lamb, 2flowing down the middle of the city’s main street. On each side of the river is the tree of life producing twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit every month of the year. Its leaves are for the healing of the nations.

3And there will no longer be any curse, and the throne of God and the Lamb will be in the city. His servants will worship him, 4and they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. 5Night will be no more, and they will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, because the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.

elements.question: What does John see flowing through the city, and what grows beside it (verses 1–2)?
elements.questionHint: Look at where the river comes from, and what the tree does.
elements.sampleAnswer: John pictures a river of living water, clear as glass, running from the seat of God and the Lamb right through the middle of the city. On either side stands the tree that gives life, carrying twelve crops of fruit, one for every month. Its leaves serve as medicine for the nations.
elements.mainPoint: **Eden is restored**: the river and tree of life, with healing for the nations.

elements.question: What is gone in verses 3–5, and what will God’s people do?
elements.questionHint: Look at the curse, the face, and the verb ‘reign’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The curse that hung over the world is gone for good. God and the Lamb rule from the city, and their servants worship God and see his face, with his name marked on them. Darkness is gone, so no lamp or sun is needed, because God himself is their light. And they will rule together for ever.
elements.mainPoint: No curse remains: God’s servants **see his face and reign**.

elements.question: In what ways does this picture complete the story that began in Eden? Think about God’s people, place and rule.
elements.questionHint: Think about who is there, where they live, and who is in charge.
elements.sampleAnswer: God’s people include people from the nations, who are his servants, worship him and see his face. The place is a new heaven and earth, a city with a river and the tree of life, which echoes the garden. And God’s rule is complete: the throne of God and the Lamb is at the centre, and his servants reign. What was lost in Eden is restored, and more, because God now lives among his people.
elements.mainPoint: The Bible ends with **God’s people** (his servants from the nations), in **God’s place** (the new heaven and earth, the city with the tree of life), under **God’s rule** (the throne of God and the Lamb), all made new.

elements.question: Which part of this picture do you most long for: the end of tears, God’s presence, healing for the nations, or something else? Why?
God says ‘I am making all things new!’ Where do you see him beginning to make things new, in your life or your church? How should this future shape the way you live now?

elements.text:
The story that began in a garden ends in a city with a garden at its heart. God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule: lost, promised, partly known, won by the King, and at last made new. We live between the King’s first coming and his return, in the part of the story where the gospel goes to the nations.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper, and see the timeline of the whole Bible.

footnotes.body: ‘Christ’ is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew ‘Messiah’. Both mean ‘anointed one’.

story.body:
When Luke’s story begins, Israel is in the land but under Roman rule. There is no king from David’s line and no prophet. Many faithful Jews are waiting for God to act: the old man Simeon is ‘looking for the restoration of Israel’ (Luke 2:25). Luke opens by saying he has investigated everything carefully and will write an orderly account (Luke 1:1–4). He wants the reader to know that these are real events in history.

The first chapters of Luke are full of echoes of the Old Testament. The angel’s words to Mary clearly recall God’s promise to David in 2 Samuel 7: a son, a throne, a kingdom without end. Mary’s own song (Luke 1:46–55) looks back to Abraham and to God’s promise to Israel. The wait is over because God has remembered his promises.

titles.body:
The angel’s three titles are packed.[[fn:1]] ‘Saviour’ recalls how God saved Israel from Egypt and from exile. ‘Christ’ says that this child is the promised king of David’s line. ‘Lord’ is a title of honour, but it is also the word that the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s name. In one sentence, the angel says that the child is the rescuer, the king and, in some sense, God himself come near.

Notice also the place: ‘the city of David’. The King is born in Bethlehem, David’s own town, as the prophet Micah had said (Micah 5:2).

genealogy.body:
Matthew and Luke both give Jesus’ family line, and they tell us different things. Matthew begins with ‘the son of David, the son of Abraham’ (Matthew 1:1), and so links Jesus to the two great promises of the Old Testament: the kingdom promised to David and the blessing promised to Abraham. Luke traces the line back much further, past Abraham to ‘Adam, the son of God’ (Luke 3:38), as if to say that Jesus’ coming concerns the whole human race.

According to early Christian tradition, Luke was a doctor and a travelling companion of Paul. He also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, which is addressed to the same Theophilus (Acts 1:1), so his two books form one continuous story from the birth of Jesus to the spread of the gospel.

thread.body: Look back to the offspring of Genesis 3:15, the family of Abraham and the house of David. Luke’s Gospel claims that all these threads meet in one child. Keep asking, through this study, how the three parts of the kingdom (people, place and rule) are being reshaped around him.

footnotes.body: Matthew’s Gospel usually says ‘the kingdom of heaven’. It means the same as ‘the kingdom of God’.

story.body:
Mark’s opening is soaked in the Old Testament. The words he quotes come from Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3, passages that promised God would come to his people. When the heavens are torn open and the Father calls Jesus ‘my Son’, an Israelite reader would recall that Israel itself had been called God’s son (Exodus 4:22), and that the king of David’s line was called God’s son too (2 Samuel 7:14).

The forty days in the wilderness also echo Israel’s forty years in the wilderness after the exodus, where the people repeatedly failed. Jesus is shown to be the true Son, who stands where Israel stood and does not fail.

kingdom.header: What does ‘the kingdom of God’ mean?
kingdom.body:
You will remember that a kingdom needs a king, a people and a place. Jesus says the kingdom of God is ‘near’[[fn:1]]: the King has come, and with him God’s rule has begun to break into the world. Through the rest of Mark’s Gospel Jesus shows that rule by healing the sick, driving out evil spirits, forgiving sins and teaching with authority.

But the kingdom is not yet complete. Jesus speaks of a kingdom that is already here and also still to come. The rest of the New Testament lives between those two points.

markglance.body:
Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels and moves at speed. It uses the word ‘immediately’ again and again, and it tells us more about what Jesus did than about what he said. The first half asks who Jesus is, and it reaches its turning point when Peter says, ‘You are the Christ’ (Mark 8:29). From then on Jesus speaks more and more about his coming suffering and death.

A key verse is Mark 10:45, where Jesus says that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, ‘and to give his life as a ransom for many’. Mark shows that the King has come, and that he wins his kingdom by giving his life. If you have time, read Mark through in one sitting. It takes about an hour.

thread.body: In the first study the Old Testament closed with the hope of a king, a servant and a Son of Man. In Mark 1 the first of those is declared in the voice from heaven, and the rest of Mark shows how Jesus takes up the other two roles as well.

footnotes.body: The Greek Old Testament calls the Hebrew Bible’s third section ‘the Writings’. Jesus here uses ‘the Psalms’ as a shorthand for it.

story.header: From the ministry to the empty tomb
story.body:
Between Mark 1 and Luke 24 lies the heart of the Gospels. Jesus’ teaching presents the kingdom: the parables, the Sermon on the Mount, the call to follow him. His miracles show the kingdom’s power over sickness, evil spirits, storms and death. Then Jesus turns towards Jerusalem and tells his disciples three times that he must suffer, be killed and rise again. They do not understand.

The crucifixion looks like the end of the story, as the Emmaus travellers’ words show. But Luke has told us in advance that this is exactly what Scripture said would happen. The death which looks like defeat is the way the King wins his kingdom.

fulfilment.body:
Old Testament promiseWhere we met itHow Christ fulfils it
The offspring who defeats the serpentGenesis 3:15 (Old Testament session 2)He shares our humanity so that through death he destroys the devil’s power (Hebrews 2:14)
Blessing for all nations through AbrahamGenesis 12:1–3 (session 3)Forgiveness is preached in his name to all nations (Luke 24:47)
LandGenesis 12:7; 15:18 (session 3)Widened to the whole world and the new creation (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:10, 16)
A king on David’s throne for ever2 Samuel 7 (session 5)The throne of his father David (Luke 1:32–33)
A servant who suffers for othersIsaiah 53 (session 7)The Christ must suffer and enter his glory (Luke 24:26)
A new creationIsaiah 65:17–25 (session 8)Christ is the first to be raised, the beginning of the new creation (1 Corinthians 15:20)

appearances.header: The risen Jesus in the rest of the New Testament
appearances.body:
Luke 24 is one of several accounts of the risen Jesus. Paul summarises the good news in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8: that Christ died for our sins and was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared to Peter and the twelve, then to more than five hundred believers at once, then to James and all the apostles, and last of all to Paul himself. Most of the five hundred were still alive when Paul wrote, so his readers could check for themselves.

The resurrection matters to the whole story. It shows that the death of Jesus was not the end of the King, and it is the first part of the new creation: Paul calls Christ ‘the firstfruits’ of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20). What happened to him will happen to his people.

thread.body: Notice that the New Testament does not tear up the Old. Jesus describes the whole Old Testament as the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms.[[fn:1]] It reads it as a story that was always heading for Christ. The remaining sessions ask what that means for the people, the place and the rule of the kingdom.

footnotes.body: Pentecost (‘fiftieth’) was the Jewish Feast of Weeks, held fifty days after Passover. It celebrated the first of the harvest.

story.body: Pentecost[[fn:1]] was the first stage in a journey that fills the rest of Acts. Jesus had told the disciples they would be his witnesses ‘in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the farthest parts of the earth’ (Acts 1:8). Acts follows that outline. The church grows in Jerusalem, the first persecution scatters believers into Judea and Samaria, and the gospel crosses a boundary when a Roman centurion, Cornelius, believes and receives the Spirit (Acts 10). A persecutor named Saul meets the risen Christ on the road to Damascus (Acts 9). As Paul, he becomes the main missionary to the non-Jewish world, and Acts ends with him preaching in Rome.

spirit.header: The Spirit and the new covenant
spirit.body:
In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people for particular tasks. The prophets, however, looked to a day when God would pour out his Spirit on all his people (Joel 2:28–32, quoted in Acts 2:17–21), and when he would put his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:26–27). That promise is closely tied to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31: a law written on hearts, and a people who know the Lord.

At Pentecost the promised Spirit comes, and Peter explains that Jesus, now exalted, has poured him out. The Spirit is the sign that the King reigns and the new covenant has begun. The people who receive him are being remade from the inside, which is exactly what Jeremiah promised.

generosity.body:
Acts 2 is not the only picture of the new community. Acts 4:32–35 describes believers who were ‘of one heart and mind’, so that no one claimed that any possession was their own and nobody among them was in need. Those who owned land or houses sold them and brought the money to the apostles, who shared it out according to need.

This generosity was not forced, and it grew out of what God had done for them. Notice what comes in the middle of the description: the apostles were giving testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus with great power (4:33). The new community lives out the new covenant promise of a changed heart, in ways that people could see. If you have time, read the whole of Acts 4:23–37.

thread.body: The first study showed that the kingdom’s three parts were damaged by sin. Here the first part is renewed: God’s people, gathered around the King and indwelt by the Spirit. The people are not defined by nation or land, but by repentance and faith in Jesus.

footnotes.body: The NET translates the Greek word in Romans 3:25 as ‘mercy seat’, the lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Other versions say ‘sacrifice of atonement’ or ‘propitiation’. All point to the place or means by which sin is dealt with and God’s anger against it is turned away.

story.body:
Romans is the most thorough explanation of the gospel in the New Testament. Paul begins with the bad news: Gentiles have rejected God in creation (Romans 1:18–32), and Jews who have the law have broken it (2:1–3:8). Everyone, he concludes, is under sin (3:9–20). Only then does he turn, in 3:21, to the good news.

Paul then uses Abraham as his example (Romans 4). Abraham was counted righteous when he believed God’s promise (Genesis 15:6), long before the law of Moses was given. The way into God’s family has always been faith in what God has promised.

images.header: Pictures of what the cross does
images.body:
The New Testament uses several pictures for what Christ’s death achieves. Each one borrows from a different part of life, and each one adds something. Romans 3 and 5 use all four.

PictureWhere it comes fromWhat it says
JustificationThe law courtThe judge declares the guilty person righteous (3:24; 5:1, 9)
RedemptionThe slave marketA price is paid to set captives free (3:24)
AtonementThe temple and its mercy seatGod displays Christ at his death as the mercy seat, where sin is dealt with (3:25)[[fn:1]]
ReconciliationBroken relationshipsEnemies are made friends (5:10–11)

abrahamfaith.body:
Paul’s argument in Romans 3 is not new. In Romans 4 he turns to Abraham to show that God has always put people right with himself in the same way. Paul quotes Genesis 15:6: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness’ (Romans 4:3). That happened long before the law of Moses was given, and before circumcision (Genesis 17), so Abraham’s standing with God did not depend on either.

Paul ends the chapter by saying that Jesus ‘was given over because of our transgressions and was raised for the sake of our justification’ (Romans 4:25). The cross deals with sin, and the resurrection shows that God has accepted what Christ did. Together they are the basis on which God declares sinners righteous.

thread.body: Isaiah 53 spoke of one wounded for the rebellion of others. Leviticus taught that sin costs a life. Paul puts these together: God himself puts Jesus forward as the means by which sin is dealt with. God can be just, because sin is punished in Christ, and he can be the one who justifies, because the penalty is borne.

footnotes.body: Some scholars think the ‘middle wall of partition’ refers to the low wall in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts, which carried warnings that trespassers risked death. Others take it as a general picture of the law that separated Jews from Gentiles. Either way, the point is the same.

story.body:
In Acts the gospel moves outward from Jerusalem. Gentiles received the Spirit without having to be circumcised, which settled the matter at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15). Paul’s letters explain why. Galatians argues that those who share Abraham’s faith are Abraham’s children. Romans looks at the place of both Jews and Gentiles in God’s plan. Ephesians shows the result: one body.

The phrase ‘middle wall of partition’ (often rendered ‘dividing wall’) may recall a real barrier in the temple in Jerusalem.[[fn:1]] Paul says that this wall has been broken down in Christ.

people.body:
It is worth noticing what Paul does not say. He does not say that Gentiles form a second people, alongside Israel. He says they are brought into the ‘citizenship of Israel’ and into God’s household. The Gentiles are joining the people of God, which is now defined by Christ.

This fits the promise made to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. It also fits Isaiah’s vision of the nations coming to the Lord’s mountain. Ephesians 2 shows what that looks like when it begins to happen.

ephesiansglance.body:
Ephesians has two halves. Chapters 1–3 describe what God has done in Christ: he has blessed believers with every spiritual blessing, chosen them before the world began, saved them by grace, and brought Jews and Gentiles together into one people. Chapters 4–6 describe how that new people should live: in unity, in holiness, and in their homes and their struggle against evil.

Just before today’s passage Paul puts grace and works together. In Ephesians 2:8–10 he says that believers are saved by grace through faith, not from works, and then adds that they are ‘created in Christ Jesus for good works’ that God prepared beforehand. Good works do not earn salvation, but they are what salvation is for. Today’s passage then shows that this new life is lived out together, as one family.

temple.body: In the first study Eden was a place where God lived with his people, and the tabernacle and temple were pictures of that. Here Paul says that God’s dwelling is a people, built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. In Christ the place and the people have come together: God’s presence is no longer tied to a building or a land, but is found wherever his people are gathered by the Spirit.

footnotes.body: Leviticus 16 describes the Day of Atonement. The high priest entered the most holy place once a year, with the blood of a bull and a goat, and a second goat, the scapegoat, was sent into the wilderness carrying the people’s sins.

story.body:
We do not know who wrote Hebrews, but we know its purpose. The first readers were Jewish Christians facing hardship, who were tempted to go back to the familiar rhythms of temple worship. The writer shows them that the Old Testament itself points beyond the old order to Christ. He draws heavily on the Psalms, on Jeremiah, and on the tabernacle and the Day of Atonement.[[fn:1]]

The letter is full of the word ‘better’: a better hope, a better covenant, a better sacrifice, a better country. It is not saying that the old things were bad. It is saying that they were shadows, and the substance has come.

shadow.body:
Hebrews 8:5 says that the earthly tabernacle was a sketch and shadow of the heavenly one. That helps to make sense of the whole Old Testament system of worship. The tabernacle, priests and sacrifices taught Israel about the holiness of God, the seriousness of sin and the need for a mediator. But they could not finally deal with sin, as the repeated sacrifices show. Hebrews 10:1–4 says it plainly.

When Jesus arrives, the shadows are replaced by the reality. He is the true high priest and the true sacrifice, and he serves in the true tent. The writer is explaining why the Old Testament’s institutions had to be fulfilled, not simply continued.

melchizedek.body:
Hebrews mentions Melchizedek several times, and many readers find him puzzling. He appears briefly in Genesis 14:18–20, when Abram returns from battle. Melchizedek is king of Salem and priest of the Most High God; he brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth of everything. Then he disappears from the story, and the only other mention in the Old Testament is a single verse in the Psalms (Psalm 110:4), which Hebrews 7:17 quotes as speaking of a king who will be ‘a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’.

Hebrews 7 says that Jesus is a priest of this kind. He did not become a priest by descent, as the Levites did, but by the power of an indestructible life (Hebrews 7:15–17). That is why his priesthood does not end, and why he can save completely those who come to God through him (7:24–25). Melchizedek points to a kind of priesthood that is greater than Aaron’s.

thread.body: Compare Hebrews 8:8–12 with Jeremiah 31:31–34 in the Old Testament study. It is one of the longest quotations of the Old Testament in the New. The writer’s point is that what Jeremiah promised has now begun. The sacrifices at Sinai and the covenant with David were always leading to this: a people with God’s law on their hearts, forgiven once for all.

footnotes.body: Revelation 20 is not part of this study. It is the chapter on which Christians differ most in their view of the end times. The study moves directly from the final victory of Christ to the new creation, which Christians agree on.

story.body:
Revelation is the last book of the Bible, and brings the whole story to its goal. It is written as a letter to seven churches, and it is full of images drawn from the Old Testament: Eden, the exodus, the temple, Daniel’s beasts and Isaiah’s new creation. John saw the risen Christ ruling over history, even when the church was under threat from the Roman empire.

The book’s central figure is the Lamb who was slain, who is also the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5–6). The Lamb has won the victory by dying, and he shares his throne with God. This is the answer to the Old Testament’s longing for a King and a servant, in a single figure. The study leaves out the middle of the book and the debated Revelation 20.[[fn:1]]

eden.body:
ThemeGenesis 2–3Revelation 21–22
God’s presenceGod moves about in the garden (3:8)The residence of God is among human beings (21:3)
WaterA river flows from Eden (2:10)The river of the water of life flows from the throne (22:1)
The tree of lifeGuarded, and the way closed (3:24)Open to all, for the healing of the nations (22:2)
The curseCursed ground, pain and death (3:14–19)No longer any curse; no more death or pain (22:3; 21:4)

place.body: The Old Testament study traced the place of the kingdom from the garden of Eden, to the promised land, to Jerusalem and the temple. The New Testament takes up all those pictures and widens them. Paul says that Abraham was promised that he would inherit the world (Romans 4:13). Hebrews says that Abraham was looking for a city with firm foundations, whose architect and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10, 16). In Revelation the city is part of a renewed heaven and earth, and God himself dwells with his people. The place has grown from a garden and a strip of land to the whole creation.

thread.body: You have now followed the whole storyline: the kingdom made, lost, promised, tasted, won and completed. The Bible’s last chapters tell us that the same God who made a garden is making all things new. Where might you go next? Pick up one of the Gospels and read it through, looking for the King, or return to a passage in either study and see how it fits the whole.

footnotes.body: The dates of Jesus’ birth and death are approximate. Most scholars place his birth a few years before 1 BC and his death between AD 30 and 33.

about.body: The Bible’s story runs across many centuries. This chart places the eight passages of this study (marked with their session numbers) in the whole sweep, and shows how the story began in the Old Testament. Dates are approximate. Genesis 1–11 gives no dates, so none are suggested for the period before Abraham.

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Notes for group leaders
intro: These studies are written for groups of about six to ten, and work for individuals too. Each session is planned for about 90 minutes; the notes suggest a shorter route if you have 60.

Aim to let the group find answers in the passage rather than hearing them from you. The sample answers show what the text contains; they are not a script, and a good answer may be put quite differently.

Each session’s notes give the aim, suggested timing, how to lead it, what to watch for, tricky points, and how the session fits the big story. The Go Deeper chapters give background you can use if the group asks for more.

aim.body: To see that the Old Testament’s promised King has arrived, and to notice how surprising the manner of his arrival is.

timing.body: Welcome and recap, 10 minutes. Opening question, 10 minutes. Luke 1:26–38, 20 minutes. Luke 2:8–14, 25 minutes. Contrast question, 10 minutes. Reflection, 10 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the contrast question, and take one reflection.

lead.body: Group members will know the Christmas story well, which is both a help and a hindrance. Ask them to read as though they have not heard it before, and to answer from the text rather than from memory. If some group members have not done the Old Testament study, take a few minutes with the recap and write ‘people, place, rule’ where everyone can see it.

watch.body: Answers drawn from carols and nativity plays rather than from Luke. For example, the passage mentions no donkey, no inn-keeper and no stable, and the shepherds’ sign is a manger. Also watch for people who find the Christmas story too familiar to engage with.

tricky.body: The virgin conception raises questions for some group members. Keep to what Luke says: the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High bring about the birth, and the child is holy and the Son of God. If someone asks how the Old Testament prepared for it, say that later sessions will build the picture.

thread.body: This session starts the story’s final stage. The three parts of the kingdom have not yet been restored, but the King is here.

aim.body: To see that Jesus’ arrival is ‘good news’ because it announces the beginning of God’s kingdom, and that it calls for repentance and faith.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Mark 1:1–15, 50 minutes. Reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 10 minutes. For 60 minutes: take the opening question briefly, and skip the question on who Jesus is.

lead.body: Read the passage aloud at Mark’s own pace: it is fast. Ask the group what they notice about how quickly Mark moves, and how little he explains. The question on who Jesus is works well as a collecting-up exercise, with answers written on a sheet.

watch.body: A view of ‘the kingdom of God’ that reduces it to heaven after death, or to a purely inward experience. Keep to the text: the kingdom is God’s rule, which Jesus announces as near, and which calls for a response now.

tricky.body: Why was Jesus baptised, since John’s baptism was for repentance? Keep this to what the passage shows: Jesus identifies with the people he has come to save, and God publicly declares him Son. Do not be drawn into detailed theories.

thread.body: The King is announcing his kingdom. The next sessions show how he wins it, and who belongs in it.

aim.body: To see that the whole Old Testament points to Christ’s suffering and resurrection, and that this gives believers a way of reading the Bible.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Luke 24:13–35, 35 minutes. Luke 24:36–49, 25 minutes. Reflection, 10 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the recognition question.

lead.body: This is the pivot of the pair of studies. Ask the group to bring to mind what they remember from the Old Testament study, and use the Go Deeper table to show how the threads come together. If the group has not done the Old Testament study, the table is a useful summary.

watch.body: A tendency to treat the Old Testament as a set of hidden predictions to be matched with Jesus’ life. Luke 24 gives a broader picture: the whole Old Testament story, with its covenants, king and sacrifices, leads to the suffering and glory of the Christ.

tricky.body: Jesus does not name particular Old Testament passages here, so the group may ask which ones he used. Do not guess. Use the table in Go Deeper for ideas, and the earlier studies. Some may also ask about the land promise (the table suggests the New Testament widens it to the world and the new creation). Keep to what the verses cited say, and do not let it become a debate.

thread.body: The resurrection is the turning point of the whole story: the King has won, and the Old Testament’s promises are being kept.

aim.body: To see that the risen Jesus reigns as Lord and Christ, and that the Spirit’s coming forms a new people of God.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Peter’s sermon, 35 minutes. The new community, 25 minutes. Reflection, 10 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the summary question.

lead.body: Read the sermon aloud as though you were Peter. Ask the group what the crowd needed to hear, and what Peter chooses to say. In the second half, let the group compare the marks of the early church with their own.

watch.body: Group members who want to spend the session on speaking in tongues or on the gifts of the Spirit. The passage’s focus is on Peter’s explanation of Jesus and the community that forms around him. Keep to that.

tricky.body: Verse 23 holds God’s plan and human guilt together without explaining how. Do not try to resolve it. The commands to repent and be baptised may raise questions about what baptism does. Say what the verse says, and leave other discussions for another occasion.

thread.body: The new covenant promise begins to be kept: a forgiven people who receive the Spirit. The next session asks how God can forgive justly.

aim.body: To see how God can forgive sinners and remain just, and to feel the weight of the love shown at the cross.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Romans 3:21–26, 35 minutes. Romans 5:1–11, 30 minutes. Reflection, 10 minutes. Prayer, 0–5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the question on verses 1–2.

lead.body: These are dense verses. Read each passage slowly, and ask the group to pick out the words they find hardest. Use the table in Go Deeper to explain redemption, justification and sacrifice by their pictures.

watch.body: The idea that justification is God overlooking sin, or a reward for good living. Verses 24–26 say God deals with sin in Christ, and gives righteousness as a gift.

tricky.body: The word in 3:25 (translated differently in different versions) and the idea of God’s wrath may trouble some. Keep to the text: God’s anger against sin is real, Christ bears what sin deserves, and the result is peace. Do not leave the group with the wrath without the love of 5:8.

thread.body: This is the answer to the question left by Isaiah 53 and Jeremiah 31: how forgiveness can be given. It is the foundation under the whole story.

aim.body: To see that the cross creates one new people of God from every background, and that the people themselves are God’s new temple.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Ephesians 2:11–22, 50 minutes. Reflection, 20 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and use only one reflection question.

lead.body: Read the passage in three parts and ask the group to say, in a sentence, what changes in each part. The reflection questions need honesty. Make sure everyone knows that people in the group may find it hard to name divisions in their own church.

watch.body: A tendency to talk about divisions in other people’s churches, rather than in our own. Gently bring the group back to the questions about their own situation. Also watch for people who treat ‘Jew and Gentile’ as a distant historical issue.

tricky.body: Questions about the future of ethnic Israel (Romans 9–11) may arise. Say that the question is a real one, that Paul discusses it elsewhere, and that this passage shows that Jews and Gentiles are united in Christ. Do not let it take over the session.

thread.body: The first part of the kingdom, a people for God, is renewed: one family from every nation. The place and the rule are reshaped around Christ.

aim.body: To see that Jesus completes the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices, and brings in the new covenant which Jeremiah promised.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Hebrews 8, 30 minutes. Hebrews 9:11–14, 25 minutes. Summary question and reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the summary question.

lead.body: Hebrews can feel technical to those who do not know Leviticus. Use the key term callout and Go Deeper to give the group the Day of Atonement in a few sentences. Then place the Jeremiah 31 text from the Old Testament study beside Hebrews 8:10–12 so that the group can see the quotation.

watch.body: The idea that the Old Testament was a mistake or a failure. Hebrews says it was a shadow: valuable, but not final. Also watch for a tendency to treat ‘obsolete’ in 8:13 as meaning ‘worthless’.

tricky.body: The statement that God found fault ‘with them’ in verse 8 (the people), and not with the covenant, can be confusing. Guide the group back to the text. Also, the sacrifice question may raise how the cross relates to the Old Testament sacrifices. The notes on Go Deeper give a short answer.

thread.body: The rule and the place of the kingdom are now located in Christ: the true priest, the true temple and the mediator of the new covenant.

aim.body: To see that the Bible ends with the full restoration of the kingdom: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule, and with God himself living among them.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 5 minutes. Revelation 21:1–8, 30 minutes. Revelation 22:1–5, 20 minutes. Summary question, 10 minutes. Reflection, 10 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and take one reflection.

lead.body: This is the end of the course, so allow time at the end to look back over the whole. Ask each person what they will take away from the course (and, if the group has done both studies, from all sixteen sessions). Use the Eden table in Go Deeper to show how the end matches the beginning. Make time to pray and to thank God for his story.

watch.body: Attempts to decode Revelation as a timetable of future events, or to draw detailed maps of the end times. Keep to what these passages say: God makes everything new, and lives with his people. Many people also find the book frightening. Reassure them that these two chapters are its destination.

tricky.body: Group members may ask about the thousand years of Revelation 20, the timing of the return of Christ or what happens to the saved and the lost. These are real questions on which Christians differ, but they are not the subject of this passage. Say that the study moves from Christ’s final victory to the new creation, and suggest that the group take such questions up on another occasion. Questions about the land promise can be met with Romans 4:13 and Hebrews 11:10 and 16, which show how the New Testament widens it.

thread.body: This is the end of the story. The three parts of the kingdom, lost in Eden and promised through the long years of the Old Testament, are brought together in Christ and made complete in the new creation.

publisher.name: BeaconLight
paras: BeaconLight is a non-denominational Christian training organisation based in the UK, founded in 1995. Its aim is to equip Christians worldwide with practically-applied Biblical gospel ministry tools — resources designed to help people both equip themselves and equip others.

BeaconLight’s resources include CrossCheck, which enables Christians to explain their faith and lead others to Jesus, and Word@Work, a verse-by-verse applied devotional commentary of the whole New Testament. BeaconLight also provides printed Biblical resources to prisons, seafarers, police, and the armed services.
BeaconLight believes that Christian ministry should be free of charge, and all its online materials are available without registration or payment. The ministry is funded entirely by donations.
BeaconLight is a member of the Evangelical Alliance and Global Connections, and is a registered charity in England and Wales (Charity No. 1047046).
